Subjects: Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Auditing outsourced LLM fine-tuning requires checking an untrusted provider's training while controlling verification cost. Uniform sampling ignores training-time signals, while checking a suspicious record can require replaying several preceding steps. We present ReplayAudit, a telemetry-guided auditing system that seals training records before challenges and independently replays sampled intervals from sealed checkpoints. Loss changes and parameter-update norms guide stratified random sampling; replay determines whether the selected computation agrees with its records. We relate sampling probabilities to replay work and evaluate the system on real LoRA training. A 7B BF16 prototype rejects a false update-norm report during a random audit; targeted checks also reject false loss reports and skipped updates. We calibrate sampling budgets offline to at least a 90% probability of directly selecting an injected step. For two learning-rate deviation settings, executing these budgets on the same honest 1.5B trajectory reduces median complete-audit wall time by 49% and 67% relative to uniform sampling. When skipped updates evade the high-anomaly stratum, the corresponding audit instead costs 38% more. These results show how deviation capture and actual replay work jointly determine the cost of telemetry-guided auditing.

[194] arXiv:2611.09612 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Kernel-Based Learning of Analytic Operators and Parametric PDEs
Giovanni S. Alberti, Markus Holzleitner, Lorenzo Rosasco, Matteo Santacesaria
Comments: 43 pages, 4 figures
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Statistics Theory (math.ST)

We study kernel-based learning of analytic operators from finite samples, with a focus on how the regularity of the target should determine the choice of the kernel. We establish embeddings of analytic operators into vector-valued reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and derive finite-sample, high-probability guarantees that quantify the uncertainty due to random sampling: in the noiseless setting, suitable analytic kernels yield rates exponential in a fractional power of the sample size, while Sobolev-type kernels yield polynomial rates. We apply the theory to the solution operator of a parametric elliptic PDE, where the training data are themselves finite-element approximations, and obtain bounds that separate the sampling and discretization contributions to the error and prescribe how the mesh size should be coupled to the sample size. The results are illustrated numerically.

[195] arXiv:2611.09615 (cross-list from cs.GT) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Contextual Search and Bilateral Trade with a Trace-Square-Root Potential
Romain Cosson, Federico Fusco, Anupam Gupta, Stefano Leonardi, Renato Paes Leme, Matteo Russo
Subjects: Computer Science and Game Theory (cs.GT); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

We present a unified potential method for contextual search and bilateral trade with one-bit feedback and obtain order-tight algorithms for both problems. Our framework starts from a Bayesian perspective in which the unknown target (for contextual search) and the unknown pair of valuations (for bilateral trade) are sampled from a known prior distribution. In that model, the decision maker bases its prediction on the posterior distribution, obtained by conditioning on feedback received in previous rounds.
For Bayesian contextual search, we present an algorithm with a total loss bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt \Sigma)$, where $\Sigma$ is the covariance matrix of the target's prior; and for contextual bilateral trade, our algorithm's regret is bounded by $O(\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{\Sigma_S}+\mathrm{Tr} \sqrt{\Sigma_B})$, where $\Sigma_S$ and $\Sigma_B$ are the covariance matrices of the seller's and buyer's valuations.
We then use ideas from this Bayesian setting and adapt a ``dual'' of this trace-square-root potential to the classical worst-case setting, where the target and valuations are chosen adversarially from the unit Euclidean ball. For both contextual search and bilateral trade, we obtain tight $O(\sqrt d)$-regret algorithms. These results match the existing lower bounds up to a constant factor and improve on the previous guarantees of $O(d\log d)$ for contextual search and of $O(d6^d)$ for bilateral trade.

[196] arXiv:2611.09634 (cross-list from cs.CL) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Steerable Multi-Objective Group-Relative Preference Optimization with Jointly Trained Low-Rank Adapters
Constantinos Karouzos, Nikolaos Aletras
Comments: Preprint. Under review
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Language model deployment often requires different trade-offs between competing objectives as user preferences change, yet standard post-training methods typically produce a single policy for a fixed objective weighting. We introduce LambdaMix, a new parameter efficient method for learning a preference conditioned family of policies with group-relative online reinforcement learning. LambdaMix jointly trains one low-rank adapter per objective over a frozen base model. One preference vector selects the adapter mixture that generates responses and weights the separately normalized rewards used to update the adapters. A single training run supports changing preferences at inference without further optimization. We experiment with four models on helpfulness and harmlessness and on solving math problems while following instructions. We also evaluate the two largest models on rewriting comments to preserve wording while reducing clues about personal attributes. On the first two tasks, LambdaMix achieves higher hypervolume than all evaluated conditioned and policy merging baselines across all four models. LambdaMix uses fewer training completions and stores fewer adapter parameters than a set of GRPO specialist policies. With architecture and initialization fixed, varying adapter mixtures and objective weights together gives wider score ranges and higher coverage than varying either alone.

[197] arXiv:2611.09642 (cross-list from eess.AS) [pdf, html, other]
Title: NAVE: A Normalized, Adaptive Conformer for Antarctic Whale Vocalization Detection
Matthias Nagl, Paul Primus, Gerhard Widmer
Comments: 5 pages, 3 figures, 2 tables. Accepted at the Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events (DCASE) 2026 Workshop. Code: this https URL
Journal-ref: Proceedings of the 11th Workshop on Detection and Classification of Acoustic Scenes and Events (DCASE 2026), Boston, USA, pp. 1-5, 2026
Subjects: Audio and Speech Processing (eess.AS); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Sound (cs.SD)

Antarctic whale vocalization detection requires temporally localizing call boundaries in long underwater recordings and classifying them into predefined call types. Training reliable machine learning models for this task is difficult due to the variability and sparsity of whale calls in passive acoustic monitoring datasets. These difficulties are further amplified by time-varying noise that can mask whale calls and by site-specific ambient sound characteristics to which a trained model may not generalize. In this work, we present NAVE, a Conformer-based detector that improves whale-call detection via three components. First, its input representation combines per-bin complex mean subtraction, which suppresses constant site-specific ambient sound characteristics, with an additional per-channel energy normalization (PCEN) channel that adapts to temporal variations in the noise floor. Second, a frequency-dynamic stem processes these noise-aware representations with convolutions that adapt across the characteristic frequency bands of the target call types. Third, we use a Conformer backbone with a convolution kernel matched to the duration of the target calls that adds an inductive bias and improves temporal localization. We evaluate NAVE on BioDCASE 2026 Task 2 using leave-one-site-out cross-validation across the validation sites, which approximates deployment on unseen recording sites. A single NAVE model with a tuned per-class threshold exceeds the stronger WhaleVAD-BPN baseline, using no boundary-proposal network and no search over post-processing parameters. A controlled ablation study shows that the normalized front-end and a duration-matched convolutional kernel each contribute substantially to recovering the D downsweep, the hardest class for previous detectors, with the wide kernel giving the largest aggregate gain.

[198] arXiv:2611.09650 (cross-list from cs.SE) [pdf, html, other]
Title: TensorMutation: Learning Weight-Space Mutations of Deep Learning Models on Neural Graphs
Zaheed Ahmed, Philip Makedonski, Jens Grabowski
Comments: 18 pages, 7 figures
Subjects: Software Engineering (cs.SE); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Mutation testing for deep learning (DL) faces a cost-realism trade-off. The pre-training approach produces realistic but computationally expensive mutants, whereas existing post-training operators modify trained models efficiently but produce mutants that less closely resemble real faults. This study asks whether the trade-off is necessary: can the weight-space effect of a fault-informed pre-training mutation operator be predicted from a trained model, without retraining it? We answer this question with TensorMutation, which represents a trained model as a neural graph and uses a mutation-conditioned graph neural network (GNN) to predict parameter changes. The GNN is trained offline and reused across unseen models so that TensorMutation can generate executable mutants without retraining. We construct a corpus of 25,252 original-mutant pairs from 71 multilayer perceptron (MLP) classifiers using 11 fault-informed pre-training operators, including 25 newly curated subjects. TensorMutation partially reproduces the behavioral effects of pre-training mutations on nine held-out subjects, and direct weight-space supervision significantly improves weight-space fidelity. On 12 real-fault subjects, TensorMutation achieves the highest median behavioral similarity among the evaluated approaches. The improvement over the post-training tool DeepMutation++ is statistically significant (Holm-adjusted p=0.018), whereas the differences from the pre-training tool DeepCrime and the norm-matched random control are not significant. These results show that fault-informed pre-training mutations leave learnable structure in weight space that transfers to unseen models.

[199] arXiv:2611.09652 (cross-list from cs.CV) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Breaking the Privacy Promise: Gradient Inversion Attacks on Federated Low-Rank Adapted Vision Transformers
Ritik K. Badiya, Siladittya Manna, Ashmit Sinha, M Yashwanth, Anirban Chakraborty
Comments: Accepted at WACV 2027
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Cryptography and Security (cs.CR); Distributed, Parallel, and Cluster Computing (cs.DC); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) has been increasingly adopted to fine-tune pretrained models with low computational cost and is therefore also preferred in the federated learning paradigm to reduce computational and communication overhead. In this work, we investigate the sparsely explored problem of the risk of private data leakage in LoRA-adapted Vision Transformers (ViTs), where low-rank updates weaken the gradient signal available to a server with access to individual client updates. We show that quality of reconstruction is limited by two coupled ambiguities: reduced information in LoRA gradients and missing spatial cues from frozen positional embeddings. To address this, we propose a spatially anchored generative inversion framework that incorporates server-prescribed trainable positional embeddings into ViT blocks during fine-tuning at clients. The resulting positional gradients act as layer-wise spatial anchors, providing additional positional cues, while the generative prior keeps reconstructions on a realistic image manifold, reducing duplicate-data and patch-permutation artifacts, {which produce similar gradients as those produced when the target client images are used}. Adding our proposed spatial anchoring to GIAS improves PSNR by 10.14 dB, SSIM by 0.45, and LPIPS by 0.098 on CIFAR-10, as well as PSNR gains of 7.83 and 11.74 dB on high-resolution CelebA and CARS datasets, respectively, in the FedSGD setting. Such gains in reconstructed image quality metrics are also maintained at higher batch sizes and in FedAvg settings. These results indicate that LoRA-based PEFT does not, by itself, prevent data leakage in FL, and carefully incorporated positional embeddings can help in exposing private information.

[200] arXiv:2611.09670 (cross-list from cs.RO) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Goodhart in the Planner: Sampling-Based Control Exploits Rewards Learned from Human Preferences
Soovadeep Bakshi, Apurba Bose
Comments: 19 pages, 4 figures. Equal contribution. Code and results will be released
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Robots increasingly choose actions by searching against a reward model learned from human preferences, in model-predictive control or best-of-$N$ selection; we measure what this does to the true objective. On HalfCheetah and Hopper with crowd-sourced labels, and on Meta-World drawer-open and plate-slide with synthetic labels and blind labels from the two authors, harder MPPI search cuts true return by up to 76%: with human labels the drawer opens in 0 of 20 runs against 10 of 10 for the cloned policy the planner starts from, while held-out label accuracy stays at 0.75-0.97. On plate-slide human labels are exploited less than synthetic ones, and on window-open search helps. True return roughly follows how far the planner's weights move from its proposals ($\sqrt{\mathrm{KL}}$) for both weighting rules we test, and best-of-$N$ with a verifier from synthetic labels falls below a single noisy action. We prove that $\chi^2$-regularized MPPI at a temperature set by the scorer's error spread on the proposals is worst-case optimal, that no positive gain can be certified once that spread exceeds the scorer's own, and that an episode's return splits exactly into per-step terms, of which the guarantee covers the selection terms. Calibrated from 100 proposal pairs ranked by true return (an oracle) on start states the evaluation never uses, this rule is the safest fix we test: with each of five independent sets it succeeds in every arm run and keeps on average 86-94% of the cloned policy's return on plate-slide and drawer-open, though it is cautious where search helps. Calibration from a person's comparisons cannot detect a bias the scorer learned from that person; correcting for the pairs people cannot tell apart, or a second person, limits the damage.

[201] arXiv:2611.09679 (cross-list from cs.RO) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Autonomous Particle Image Velocimetry Using Zero-Shot Sim-to-Real Reinforcement Learning
Chang Rajani, Luke Sebastien Marsden, Stephan Kunz, Claudio Mucignat, Ivan Lunati
Comments: 9 pages
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Particle image velocimetry (PIV) reconstructs a flow field from the motion of tracer particles but the reconstruction quality is bounded by how well the flow structure of interest is resolved in the images. The acquisition position is typically fixed by the operator before the measurement. We cast camera placement as a sequential decision-making problem and train a reinforcement learning agent to control a 6-DoF manipulator equipped with a camera, enabling it to locate, frame and resolve a hydrofoil wake in a water tunnel. The agent commands the camera pose and observes the scene only through the velocity field and uncertainty estimated from time-separated image pairs. It is trained entirely in a photorealistic simulation of our water tunnel, with wakes generated by Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulations of hydrofoils with varying profiles, positions and angles of attack. After zero-shot transfer to the real water tunnel, the policy reliably locates and frames the wakes of randomly placed hydrofoils. It resolves the wake at a higher resolution than a fixed camera view and with lower error in the measured flow statistics, in roughly half the time of a full scan and with far fewer image pairs.

[202] arXiv:2611.09701 (cross-list from stat.ML) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Where Should Learning Live? Regret Analysis for Text, Parameter, and Joint Adaptation
Jungtaek Kim, Jaden Park, Jongwon Jeong, Emmanouil-Vasileios Vlatakis-Gkaragkounis, Kangwook Lee
Subjects: Machine Learning (stat.ML); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Language-model systems can select prompts and parameter adapters repeatedly during deployment, using feedback to guide later choices. Earlier choices may change the context or environment inherited by later configurations. We study selection among preconstructed candidates and compare cumulative loss with the best fixed prompt--parameter pair used from the beginning. This excess loss separates into three terms: selection regret within the available family, the gap from restricting that family, and the benefit or harm of the actual deployment history. Selection is evaluated using the history each candidate would have produced if used throughout, which separates candidate quality from the effects of switching. When loss functions are fixed independently of selector randomness, past choices affect loss for only a bounded number of rounds, and every candidate's own-history loss is revealed, limiting switches yields sublinear expected regret within the selected family. We also quantify the costs and additional assumptions of independent probing and deployment-only feedback. Controlled experiments show that fewer switches can either lower or raise deployed loss, depending on whether inherited histories are harmful or helpful. With Qwen3.5-9B on Spider, text-only selection has lower within-family regret than joint selection, yet produces more failures because its candidate family excludes stronger configurations.

[203] arXiv:2611.09715 (cross-list from cs.AI) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Intent-Aware Caching for Efficient LLM Serving
Kazi Hasan Ibn Arif, JinYi Yoon, Dimitrios S. Nikolopoulos, Hans Vandierendonck, Deepu John, Bo Ji
Comments: NeurIPS 2026 | Code: this https URL
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Modern LLM serving systems use prefix caching to accelerate multi-turn conversational workloads. They cache the key-value states of previous conversation prefixes and reuse them when subsequent requests share the same prefix, to avoid redundant prefill computation and reduce serving latency. However, achieving a high cache hit rate remains challenging because cache reuse depends on whether a conversation continues and how soon the next turn arrives. Our analysis of real workloads shows that user intent is a useful signal for this behavior, as different intents exhibit different continuation probabilities and inter-turn delays. Based on this key insight, we propose Intent-Aware Caching (IAC), an online eviction policy that classifies requests by intent, learns lightweight reuse statistics from recent serving logs and leverages these statistics to guide an oracle-inspired eviction strategy. Extensive evaluation on real workloads (WildChat and ShareChat) shows that IAC reaches a 34.6% cache hit rate. This substantially outperforms both the previous learning-based approach (18.8%) and traditional methods such as least recently used (LRU, 12.2%), while reducing average serving latency by up to 46.1%.

[204] arXiv:2611.09785 (cross-list from cs.CL) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Are These Programmers Ripe Enough to Eat? Evaluating How LLMs Handle Lexical Knowledge Conflicts in Translation
Dongxu Wu, Sara Court, Micha Elsner
Subjects: Computation and Language (cs.CL); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

External lexical resources can help large language models (LLMs) translate texts in low-resource languages and specialized domains, but these resources may conflict with models' prior lexical knowledge. To isolate this conflict, we construct a controlled Mandarin-to-English translation task in which familiar source words are assigned new meanings within and across semantic categories. We treat these prompt-supplied meanings as contextual knowledge (CK) and systematically evaluate the effects of word frequency, sentence context, and prompt framing on the translated outputs. Across nine models, CK reliance is greater for less frequent source words and in sentence contexts that support the supplied meanings. Prompt framing can reduce CK reliance, but seven of nine models favor CK even when explicitly instructed to ignore the supplied meanings. Within model families, larger models are more likely than smaller models to utilize CK in their outputs. Three follow-up experiments further show that modal weakening lowers CK reliance, the effect of repetition depends on prompt layout, and the effect of reasoning varies across models. Overall, our controlled study reveals how CK reliance varies across conditions and models, motivating new methods to detect and evaluate lexical conflicts and guide models' lexical choices in LLM-based translation.

[205] arXiv:2611.09792 (cross-list from cs.AI) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Knowing When to Intervene: Causal Evaluation of AI Agents
Ayush Sawarni, Wenqian Xing, Tijana Zrnic, Ramesh Johari, Vasilis Syrgkanis
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG); Econometrics (econ.EM); Methodology (stat.ME)

Current evaluations of agentic AI systems primarily rely on benchmarks. However, the static nature of benchmarks makes them uninformative about the value of auditing interventions at deployment time. For reliable deployment, we often need to determine within an agent's trajectory whether or not to intervene, e.g., by verifying the agent's current output or steering it toward different behavior, using either human review or more costly models or time-consuming agentic supervision. The value of such interventions is fundamentally a causal inference question, asking whether the causal effect of such an intervention is beneficial for the final outcome. Estimating this causal effect is particularly challenging due to the dynamic nature of the problem: the impact of an intervention depends on the current context and environment, as well as the agent's future behavior. We develop the first methodologically grounded framework for evaluating the causal effects of randomized interventions within agent trajectories. By leveraging a relatively small dataset of agent trajectories collected under randomized interventions such as verification or screening, we can estimate the dynamic causal effect of a rich class of (contextual) intervention policies. The structural parameters that we estimate can also be used to construct safety leaderboards that capture the risk of various agentic actions, which can be used by practitioners for audit prioritization. Applying our methods to tau-bench Retail, ToolSandbox, and ImpossibleBench, we find that intervention effects vary substantially across agent actions and states. More broadly, our work suggests a rich research agenda at the intersection of causal inference and agentic evaluation, which we believe is essential for the reliable and safe deployment of AI agents in the real world.

[206] arXiv:2611.09817 (cross-list from hep-lat) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Machine learning for lattice QCD
Gurtej Kanwar, Scott Lawrence, Alessandro Nada, Phiala Shanahan
Comments: 47 pages, 5 figures
Subjects: High Energy Physics - Lattice (hep-lat); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Machine learning (ML) methods have been explored as a means of optimizing lattice field theory calculations, with increasing interest in recent years. This chapter gives an introduction and summary to the use of ML methods to optimize lattice field theory without introducing any uncontrolled approximations. We focus on those directions which are clearly established as of late 2025, marking the 50th anniversary of the beginning of the study of lattice gauge theory. This chapter is a contribution to the online book ``Lattice QCD at 50 years,'' (LQCD@50), edited by Tanmoy Bhattacharya, Maarten Golterman, Rajan Gupta, Laurent Lellouch, and Steve Sharpe.

[207] arXiv:2611.09818 (cross-list from cs.AI) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Generative Latent Priors for Interpreting and Steering Protein Language Models
Daniel Hinjos, Lucía Urcelay
Comments: Accepted at the Interpretability for Discovery (Interp4Discovery) Workshop at the 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026)
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Dominant methods for interpreting large models impose strong structural assumptions. Generative Latent Priors (GLP) are a complementary approach: a diffusion model that learns the distribution of a frozen model's activations directly, imposing no assumptions. We port GLP to ESM-2 activations (UniRef50) and evaluate it at two host scales (ESM-2-8M and -650M), both as a lens for protein representations and as a prior for editing them. Generation quality scales smoothly with depth and compute. As a lens, single GLP "meta-neurons" are the strongest probes of discrete Swiss-Prot concepts at both hosts, beating InterPLM's released SAE features, and lead on continuous properties at 8M though not at 650M; falsification tests show this is mostly concentration, not new information. As an editing prior, the on-manifold correction makes DiffMean steering of three biochemical properties effective and restores on-manifoldness, but only in isolation: re-embedding the sequences actually produced after several rounds of decoding, the structural plausibility is compromised. This is mainly reproduced in additional SAE-based clamping structural steering experiments, where only Helix motif succeeds. The naturalness failure is traced to the rewriting coverage and the decoder rather than the prior, highlighting what the method must clear before it can serve for both discovery-by-editing and discovery-by-exploration. Trained GLPs are released on this http URL.

[208] arXiv:2611.09836 (cross-list from cs.AI) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Can Agentic Systems Close the Gap in Radiology with Production AI Tools?
Aubin Charley, Julien Khlaut, Charles Corbière, Pierre Manceron, Corentin Dancette, Léo Machado
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Radiology AI has developed along two paths: specialized models that perform well on narrow tasks but cover few clinical findings, and generalist models that address a broader range of tasks but remain prone to hallucination and inaccurate measurements. Combining the two through agentic systems offers a route towards comprehensive radiology reporting, but published systems are tied to one modality or body part. We describe a radiology agentic framework that standardizes how an orchestrator calls modular tools to produce a structured report, and use it to measure what such a system can do with the tools from FDA-cleared radiology AI devices. Report generation is simulated on a large multi-modality report corpus, with the orchestrator given either a catalog of finding classes consolidated from the cleared devices, each available on the modalities it is cleared for, or an unlimited catalog in which any class can be requested, and planning either from the clinical indication or from the target report. Tool outputs are simulated from the reference report, so the comparison isolates tool availability and orchestration from tool error. With the cleared catalog and the indication alone, the orchestrator recovers under a third of the clinically actionable findings; recovery improves substantially with the unlimited catalog, and further when the plan is written from the target report. Attributing every missed finding to a cause shows that most are classes no cleared device offers for the study's modality, and that a third are classes or tools that were offered and not called. Adding the most frequently missing tools closes most of the gap to the unlimited catalog on held-out reports, whereas a smaller orchestrator with the unlimited catalog gives up the whole gain. Tool availability and effective orchestration are thus complementary constraints on comprehensive AI-assisted radiology reporting.

[209] arXiv:2611.09863 (cross-list from cs.AI) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Flow-Guided Target-Space Alignment via Path Consistency
Ruizhi Yuan, Zeqiu Yu, Wei Gao, Wei Chen, Xiwei Tang, Lu Tang
Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Many multimodal alignment problems require mapping a source modality into a fixed space defined by a target modality, where the target space is not merely an intermediate embedding but is used directly for downstream analysis. In this setting, successful alignment should preserve both the global structure of the target distribution and the instance-level correspondence observed in paired source--target training data. Existing objectives typically address only part of this goal: contrastive losses encourage relative similarity, distribution-matching losses improve marginal agreement, and pointwise regression fits each source sample to its paired target without explicitly modeling target-space path geometry. We propose FlowAlign, a flow-guided target-space alignment method that repurposes conditional flow matching as a training-time alignment signal rather than an inference-time transport model. FlowAlign uses the learned flow field to guide the alignment of source-side representations with the fixed target space, encouraging them to preserve paired correspondence while remaining compatible with the global target-space structure. We further provide theoretical analysis showing how FlowAlign helps improve paired correspondence by controlling endpoint accuracy and capturing local target-space geometry. Experiments on synthetic data, paired single-cell multiome benchmarks, and image--text alignment demonstrate that FlowAlign improves instance level correspondence while preserving target-space structure across different modality settings.

[210] arXiv:2611.09864 (cross-list from cs.RO) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Grasp-TAGS: Task-Aware Grasp Selection via Critic Distillation for Prehensile Loco-Manipulation
Xun Tu, Minghao Zou, Karthik Desingh
Comments: 10 pages, 6 figures
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Loco-manipulation, which requires mobile manipulators to coordinate locomotion and manipulation over long horizons, is a key capability for large-object rearrangement in applications such as service robotics and warehouse automation. Despite recent progress, reliably executing these tasks remains challenging because performance depends on complex robot-object and object-environment interaction dynamics. Existing approaches address this challenge either through model-based methods, which often require accurate dynamics models, or through learning-based methods, which reduce this requirement but typically assume a fixed or predefined initial grasp. However, different geometrically stable grasps can lead to substantially different downstream manipulation performance. Therefore, we propose Grasp-TAGS, a task-aware grasp selection framework for goal-conditioned large-object rearrangement. We train a unified PPO-based reinforcement learning policy across multiple initial grasp configurations and distill the learned critic into a lightweight grasp utility network that ranks candidate grasps using only the candidate grasp configuration and goal information. At inference time, we select the grasp with the highest predicted downstream utility for the downstream policy to complete the task, before even making a contact. Experiments demonstrate that Grasp-TAGS improves rearrangement success over both fixed single-grasp policies and random grasp selection, achieving an average success rate of 89.84% compared with 79.87% for the best-performing single-grasp policies, an improvement of 9.97 percentage points. Grasp-TAGS also reduces final orientation errors across all evaluated objects. For more qualitative results, refer to the supplementary webpage: this https URL

[211] arXiv:2611.09878 (cross-list from cs.CV) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Graded convolutional networks: scale invariance without the scale and robustness to unknown blur
Tanush Shaska
Comments: 26 pages, 2 figures, 7 tables. Code, trained networks and results: this https URL
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

The Gaussian jet of an image is a graded vector space: a dilation by $\lambda$ multiplies derivatives of order $k$ by $\lambda^{-k}$. Local graded convolutions are exactly homogeneous differential operators, and a local feature is dilation-invariant if and only if it factors through the scale-normalized jet or, without the scale, through the retraction onto the weighted sphere of the grading. Under unknown Gaussian blur the retraction changes only by a change of scale, whereas the scale-normalized jet acquires a grading factor that no radial normalization removes. At the zero jet the retraction separates image families that radial normalizations and continuous classifiers cannot. Networks built on the retraction are universal for invariant features. On MNIST such a network keeps 88.4% accuracy under a two-pixel blur, against 66.2% for the same network on scale-normalized derivatives; in Lindeberg's Gaussian derivative network the retraction raises accuracy at that blur from 91.5% to 95.1%.

[212] arXiv:2611.09882 (cross-list from cs.CV) [pdf, html, other]
Title: FlowMoP: Stochastic Multi-Person Motion Prediction
Aadya Agrawal, Ho Kei Cheng, Alexander Schwing
Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026. 22 pages, including references and appendix
Subjects: Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Predicting the future motion of multiple people is inherently stochastic: the same observed history admits many plausible continuations depending on intent, coordination, and social context. Yet the dominant paradigm in multi-person 3D motion prediction remains deterministic, with existing methods producing a fixed number of outputs per agent. In contrast, we present a conditional flow matching framework that jointly generates diverse future motions for multiple agents, modeling both global trajectories and root-relative poses. A B-spline reparameterization compresses the generative state space while enforcing temporal smoothness, and a dual-stream transformer conditions each agent's predictions on observed neighbor motion for interaction-aware forecasting. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance on CMU-Mocap (UMPM) and 3DPW, outperforming deterministic baselines on joint position error, pose error, and final displacement error despite producing a full predictive distribution. We additionally establish the first motion prediction baseline on WorldPose, a large-scale professional soccer dataset, where social conditioning demonstrably concentrates predictive uncertainty along interaction-constrained directions.

[213] arXiv:2611.09892 (cross-list from cs.RO) [pdf, html, other]
Title: On Agentic Manipulation Policies
Chen Chen, Omid Bagherieh, Naveen Nikamanth Appiah Balaji, Jesse T. Gonzalez, Negin Heravi, Fahad Islam, Xueting Li, Jean-Baptiste Regli, Kejia Ren, Petr Švec, David J. Yoon, Matthias Müller, Vladlen Koltun
Comments: Videos and code available at: this https URL
Subjects: Robotics (cs.RO); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV); Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Recent work on robot manipulation has focused on specialist policies trained on demonstrations. We show that generalist AI models can control manipulators more reliably than specialist policies such as vision-language-action models (VLAs) and world-action models (WAMs). We systematically analyze agentic manipulation policies (AMPs), in which a generalist AI model commands the manipulator directly, adapting its actions as the task unfolds. We present AMP1, a reference harness that runs unchanged across single-arm, bimanual, and mobile manipulation. AMP1 achieves state-of-the-art results on the RoboLab-120 and CaP-Gym benchmarks, with no demonstrations or task-specific training. On RoboLab-120, AMP1 reaches an 85.6\% success rate zero-shot, compared to 49.2\% and 42.9\% for leading VLA and WAM policies. The agent succeeds zero-shot in 104 of 108 real-world trials spanning twelve tasks and three robot instances, reducing failure rates by 20x and 15x relative to strong VLA and WAM baselines. The basic harness supplies no grasping, pushing, or placing skills; the agent develops its own strategies, such as searching for hidden objects, using objects as tools, and calibrating its cameras. With the addition of a persistent memory store, the agent can also learn from experience: an augmented harness with a memory representation that is carried across episodes lowers the failure rate on RoboDojo bimanual manipulation tasks by 4.6x relative to zero-shot deployment. Our analysis suggests that AMPs are substantially more general and robust than specialist manipulation policies, providing a promising foundation for robot manipulation.

Replacement submissions (showing 204 of 204 entries)

[214] arXiv:2306.13275 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: A Theoretical Bridge Between Long-Tailed Recognition and Continual Learning
Mahdiyar Molahasani, Michael Greenspan, Ali Etemad
Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

We theoretically and empirically establish a previously unexplored connection between Long-Tailed Recognition (LTR) and Continual Learning (CL). Specifically, we show that training on a long-tailed dataset with imbalance factor $\mathrm{IF}$ drives model parameters into an $O(1/\sqrt{\mathrm{IF}})$ neighborhood of the dominant-class solution, under both uniform and exponentially decaying cardinality distributions. Building on this result, we establish an objective-level reformulation of LTR as a sequential learning problem and prove that the CL objective upper-bounds the balanced LTR loss up to a constant determined by the residual Head loss. Motivated by this connection, we introduce Continual Learning for Long-Tailed Recognition (CLTR), a principled framework that leverages standard off-the-shelf CL methods to sequentially learn Head and Tail classes while mitigating catastrophic forgetting. Extensive experiments on CIFAR100-LT, CIFAR10-LT, ImageNet-LT, and Caltech256 validate our theoretical predictions and demonstrate strong performance across diverse LTR benchmarks. In the foundation-model regime, CLTR with DualPrompt on a CLIP backbone outperforms standard adaptation baselines and is competitive with specialized methods using external semantic supervision. Our work bridges LTR and CL both theoretically and empirically, providing a principled approach for addressing long-tailed learning using standard CL strategies.

[215] arXiv:2501.19040 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Towards the Worst-case Robustness of Large Language Models
Huanran Chen, Zeming Wei, Yao Huang, Yinpeng Dong, Jun Zhu
Comments: Accepted by TMLR
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Recent studies have revealed the vulnerability of large language models to adversarial attacks, where adversaries craft specific inputs to induce incorrect or harmful outputs. Although various empirical defenses have been proposed, their worst-case robustness remains poorly understood, raising concerns about how they would behave against stronger future attacks. Here, we study the worst-case robustness of LLMs from both empirical and theoretical perspectives. First, we provide tighter empirical upper bounds for the tested deterministic defenses using stronger white-box attacks, under which most tested configurations achieve nearly 0\% robustness. Second, we formulate randomized-smoothing certification for bounded and binary base functions as fractional and 0-1 knapsack problems, respectively, and derive grouped solvers for two token kernels. For example, on AdvBench, we certify a GPT-4o safety detector smoothed by a uniform kernel to an average certified $\ell_0$ radius of 2.02. In our stated suffix-attack setting, the same kernel certifies a Llama-3-8B safety detector to an average certified radius of 6.41.

[216] arXiv:2505.23086 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Equivariant Spherical Transformer for Efficient Molecular Modeling
Junyi An, Xinyu Lu, Yunfei Shi, Peijia Lin, Licheng Xu, Qianwei Tang, Chao Qu, Fenglei Cao, Yuan Qi
Comments: 31 pages, 5 figures
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Equivariant Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have significantly advanced the modeling of 3D molecular structure by leveraging group representations. However, message passing built only from exactly equivariant operations can have restricted practical expressiveness at a fixed representation degree. We introduce the Equivariant Spherical Transformer (EST), a plug-and-play module that applies Transformer attention to spherical spatial representations obtained from group representations. EST explicitly mixes information across sampled orientations, unlike prior orientation-wise spherical operations, while retaining a strong approximate equivariant inductive bias through near-uniform spherical sampling. As demonstrated by our experiments on challenging benchmarks like OC20, MPtrj and QM9, EST-based models achieve state-of-the-art performance. For the complex molecular systems within OC20, small models empowered by EST can outperform some larger models and those using additional data. We characterize the ideal closed-domain condition under which the continuous operation is exactly equivariant and empirically quantify the finite-sampling accuracy--equivariance--memory trade-off used in practice.

[217] arXiv:2505.24030 (replaced) [pdf, other]
Title: From Images to Signals: Are Large Vision Models Useful for Time Series Analysis?
Ziming Zhao, ChengAo Shen, Hanghang Tong, Dongjin Song, Zhigang Deng, Qingsong Wen, Jingchao Ni
Comments: The manuscript has been withdrawn by the authors to undergo substantial revisions. A thoroughly revised version will be submitted in the future
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Transformer-based models have gained increasing attention in time series research, driving interest in Large Language Models (LLMs) and foundation models for time series analysis. As the field moves toward multi-modality, Large Vision Models (LVMs) are emerging as a promising direction. In the past, the effectiveness of Transformer and LLMs in time series has been debated. When it comes to LVMs, a similar question arises: are LVMs truely useful for time series analysis? To address it, we design and conduct the first principled study involving 4 LVMs, 8 imaging methods, 18 datasets and 26 baselines across both high-level (classification) and low-level (forecasting) tasks, with extensive ablation analysis. Our findings indicate LVMs are indeed useful for time series classification but face challenges in forecasting. Although effective, the contemporary best LVM forecasters are limited to specific types of LVMs and imaging methods, exhibit a bias toward forecasting periods, and have limited ability to utilize long look-back windows. We hope our findings could serve as a cornerstone for future research on LVM- and multimodal-based solutions to different time series tasks.

[218] arXiv:2506.02864 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: BNPO: Beta Normalization Policy Optimization
Changyi Xiao, Mengdi Zhang, Yixin Cao
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Reinforcement learning with rule-based, binary-valued reward functions has been shown to significantly enhance the reasoning capabilities of large language models. These models typically rely on REINFORCE-based policy optimization methods, such as REINFORCE with baseline and group relative policy optimization (GRPO). However, a key limitation is that existing methods either ignore reward normalization or use static normalization schemes, which fail to adapt to the evolving policy during training. This mismatch can lead to unstable gradient estimates and hinder training stability. To address this issue, we propose Beta Normalization Policy Optimization (BNPO), a novel method that adaptively normalizes rewards using a Beta distribution with dynamically updated parameters. By aligning normalization with the changing policy distribution, BNPO enables more accurate, lower-variance gradient estimation and promotes stable training dynamics. We provide theoretical analysis showing that BNPO reduces variance and generalizes both REINFORCE and GRPO under binary-valued rewards. In addition, we introduce an advantage decomposition mechanism to extend BNPO to more complex reward settings. Experimental results demonstrate that BNPO achieves state-of-the-art performance among policy optimization methods on reasoning tasks.

[219] arXiv:2506.06784 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Caterpillar GNN: Replacing Message Passing with Graph-Level Aggregation
Marek Černý
Comments: Accepted for NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Message-passing graph neural networks (MPGNNs) dominate modern graph learning. Typical efforts enhance MPGNN's expressive power by enriching the adjacency-based aggregation. In contrast, we introduce a graph-level aggregation over walk incidence-based matrices that are constructed to deliberately trade off some expressivity for stronger and more structured inductive bias. This approach allows for gradual scaling between classical message-passing and simpler methods based on walks. Drawing on weighted automata, we ensure our gradual scaling is polynomial-time and avoids the combinatorial explosion of colored walks. Our second result characterizes the expressive power at each scale using homomorphism counts over a hierarchy of generalized caterpillar graphs. Based on these foundations, we propose Caterpillar GNNs that substantially reduce the number of nodes in the hidden layers of the computational graphs on real-world datasets. This gradual reduction does not obstruct learning, enabling a systematic study of lower-order expressivity. We further describe benchmark settings where task-aligned expressivity supports learning.

[220] arXiv:2507.15079 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging for uncertainty quantification of electricity price forecasts
Arkadiusz Lipiecki, Bartosz Uniejewski
Comments: Preprint
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Statistical Finance (q-fin.ST); Applications (stat.AP)

Quantifying the uncertainty of forecasting models is essential to assess and mitigate the risks associated with data-driven decisions, especially in volatile domains such as electricity markets. In this paper, we propose a computationally efficient isotonic variant of Quantile Regression Averaging (QRA), called Isotonic Quantile Regression Averaging (iQRA), for generating probabilistic forecasts from ensembles of point forecasts. Building on QRA, we introduce stochastic order constraints as a hyperparameter-free regularization mechanism that reduces computational complexity while maintaining competitive forecast accuracy. We further demonstrate that the same isotonic regularization principle can be applied to the smoothed estimator of QRA. In an extensive forecasting study of two European day-ahead electricity markets, we show that iQRA and its smoothed variant consistently rank among the top state-of-the-art postprocessing methods in terms of reliability and sharpness. It produces well-calibrated prediction intervals, with smoothed iQRA providing superior reliability even when compared against coverage-oriented conformal prediction. We further introduce a battery arbitrage evaluation, showing that the leading probabilistic methods achieve the highest profit per trade and that probabilistic risk control improves the economic value of trading decisions. Isotonic regularization offers a scalable hyperparameter-free variable selection for linear quantile regression, making iQRA attractive for practical decision-support systems in energy markets.

[221] arXiv:2509.00031 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: End-to-End On-Device Quantization-Aware Training for LLMs at Inference Cost
Qitao Tan, Xiaoying Song, Ningxi Cheng, Guoming Li, Jun Liu, Lingzi Hong, Caiwen Ding, Jundong Li, Xiaoming Zhai, Shaoyi Huang, Jin Lu, Ninghao Liu, Wei Niu, Geng Yuan
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Quantization reduces the deployment cost of large language models (LLMs). However, post-training quantization (PTQ) cannot fine-tune model parameters and often degrades accuracy in low-bit settings, while quantization-aware training (QAT) requires backpropagation and incurs high memory overhead. We propose ZeroQAT, a zeroth-order QAT framework supporting both weight and activation quantization. By using forward-only gradient estimation, ZeroQAT removes backpropagation and substantially reduces memory and computation while retaining end-to-end optimization benefits. We further introduce a lightweight variant of ZeroQAT for quantized fine-tuning, which freezes and pre-quantizes most parameters to further cut memory usage. Experiments show that ZeroQAT consistently outperforms representative PTQ and QAT baselines while requiring significantly less memory. For example, ZeroQAT enables fine-tuning of a 13B model at extremely low bit-widths (e.g., 2-4 bits) on a single 8GB GPU, and even allows fine-tuning a 6.7B model on a OnePlus 12 smartphone, demonstrating its practicality for end-to-end QAT on resource-limited edge devices.

[222] arXiv:2509.17228 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Causal Representation Learning from Multimodal Clinical Records under Non-Random Modality Missingness
Zihan Liang, Ziwen Pan, Ruoxuan Xiong
Comments: To appear in Proc. of EMNLP 2025 (21 pages)
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Computation and Language (cs.CL); Methodology (stat.ME)

Clinical notes contain rich patient information, such as diagnoses or medications, making them valuable for patient representation learning. Recent advances in large language models have further improved the ability to extract meaningful representations from clinical texts. However, clinical notes are often missing. For example, in our MIMIC-IV cohort, 35.15% of patients have no eligible discharge summaries. In such cases, representations can be learned from other modalities such as structured data, chest X-rays, or radiology reports. Yet the availability of these modalities is influenced by clinical decision-making and varies across patients, potentially producing modality missing-not-at-random (MMNAR) patterns. We propose a causal representation learning framework that leverages observed data and informative missingness in multimodal clinical records. It consists of: (1) an MMNAR-aware modality fusion component that integrates structured data, imaging, and text while conditioning on missingness patterns to capture patient health and clinician-driven assignment; (2) a modality reconstruction component with latent alignment to preserve modality information in the learned representation; and (3) a multitask outcome prediction model with a rectifier that corrects for residual bias from specific modality observation patterns. Comprehensive evaluations across MIMIC-IV and eICU show consistent gains over the strongest baselines, achieving relative AUC improvements of up to 4.3% for hospital readmission and 2.7% for ICU admission.

[223] arXiv:2510.03086 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Chaining 2-FWL GNNs for Combinatorial Graph Alignment
Marc Lelarge
Comments: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

For the combinatorial graph alignment problem (GAP), finding the node correspondence that maximizes the number of common edges (nce) between two unlabeled graphs, the classical Frank-Wolfe heuristic FAQ remains a strong baseline once it is properly initialized, while existing GNN approaches struggle in the purely structural setting. We introduce a chaining procedure: a sequence of Folklore-type (2-FWL) GNNs in which each network is trained with cross-entropy after decoding the previous network's similarity matrix and ranking nodes by their current alignment quality. This non-differentiable ranking step injects discrete combinatorial feedback at every stage; at inference, we iterate the final network and keep the candidate with highest observed nce. On sparse Erdos-Renyi graphs at noise level 0.25, chained FGNNs used to initialize FAQ reach 85% accuracy versus 13% for FAQ initialized from the convex relaxation, and essentially 0% for prior GNN methods. On correlated regular graphs, where MPNNs with constant features produce identical node embeddings (1-WL fails to refine) and FAQ's convex initialization is degenerate, chaining is the only method among those we evaluate, including Gromov-Wasserstein solvers, that recovers a non-trivial alignment. On three real-world benchmarks (yeast PPI, coauthorship, and road networks), recent comparisons underestimate FAQ by initializing it from a uniform doubly stochastic matrix; initialized from the convex relaxation it already surpasses prior reported numbers, and dataset-specific chained FGNNs further improve on this strengthened baseline. Code and pretrained chains available at: this https URL.

[224] arXiv:2510.04606 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Closed-Form Last Layer Optimization
Alexandre Galashov, Nathaël Da Costa, Liyuan Xu, Philipp Hennig, Arthur Gretton
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Neural networks are typically optimized with variants of stochastic gradient descent. Under a squared loss, however, the optimal solution to the linear last layer weights is known in closed-form. We propose to leverage this during optimization, treating the last layer as a function of the backbone parameters, and optimizing solely for these parameters. We show this is equivalent to alternating between gradient descent steps on the backbone and closed-form updates on the last layer. We adapt the method for the setting of stochastic gradient descent, by trading off the loss on the current batch against the accumulated information from previous batches. We provide theoretical analyses showing convergence of the method to an optimal solution in the neural tangent kernel regime, as well as quantifying the gains compared to standard SGD in a one-step analysis. Finally, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach compared with SGD and Adam on a squared loss in several regression tasks, including neural operators and causal inference.

[225] arXiv:2510.08369 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Guided Star-Shaped Masked Diffusion
Viacheslav Meshchaninov, Egor Shibaev, Artem Makoian, Ivan Klimov, Nikita Balagansky, Daniil Gavrilov, Aibek Alanov, Dmitry Vetrov
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

The performance of pre-trained masked diffusion models is often constrained by their sampling procedure, which makes decisions irreversible and struggles in low-step generation regimes. We introduce a novel sampling algorithm that works with pre-trained models and, after a lightweight fine-tuning of a single layer, significantly improves sample quality and efficiency. Our method reformulates the generation process using a star-shaped paradigm, which inherently allows for error correction. To make this process effective, we augment it with a learnable re-masking scheduler that intelligently identifies and revises likely errors. This approach yields a substantial quality boost, particularly when using a small number of sampling steps. We extensively ablate key components of our approach and show its usability in different scenarios. In comprehensive experiments on text, and code generation, our sampling algorithm outperforms or matches existing methods.

[226] arXiv:2510.09034 (replaced) [pdf, other]
Title: Convergence of optimizers implies eigenvalues filtering at equilibrium
Jerome Bolte (TSE-R), Quoc-Tung Le (DAO), Edouard Pauwels (TSE-R)
Journal-ref: Transactions on Machine Learning Research 2025, 19 p
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Dynamical Systems (math.DS); Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Ample empirical evidence in deep neural network training suggests that a variety of optimizers tend to find nearly global optima. In this article, we adopt the reversed perspective that convergence to an arbitrary point is assumed rather than proven, focusing on the consequences of this assumption. From this viewpoint, in line with recent advances on the edge-of-stability phenomenon, we argue that different optimizers effectively act as eigenvalue filters determined by their hyperparameters. Specifically, the standard gradient descent method inherently avoids the sharpest minima, whereas Sharpness-Aware Minimization (SAM) algorithms go even further by actively favoring wider basins. Inspired by these insights, we propose two novel algorithms that exhibit enhanced eigenvalue filtering, effectively promoting wider minima. Our theoretical analysis leverages a generalized Hadamard--Perron stable manifold theorem and applies to general semialgebraic $C^2$ functions, without requiring additional non-degeneracy conditions or global Lipschitz bound assumptions. We support our conclusions with numerical experiments on feed-forward neural networks.

[227] arXiv:2511.20798 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Physics Steering: Causal Control of Cross-Domain Concepts in a Physics Foundation Model
Rio Alexa Fear, Payel Mukhopadhyay, Michael McCabe, Alberto Bietti, Miles Cranmer
Comments: 16 Pages, 9 Figures. Code available at this https URL
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computational Physics (physics.comp-ph)

Foundation models trained on text and images have been shown to develop abstract internal features that align with human concepts and that can be directly manipulated via activation steering to alter model behaviour. Whether scientific foundation models learn similarly abstract and domain-general representations has remained an open question. Inspired by recent work identifying single directions in activation space that control complex behaviours in large language models, we show that Walrus, a large physics foundation model, learns linearly steerable representations of physical phenomena. By computing the difference between activations representing contrasting physical regimes, we identify single directions in activation space that correspond to vorticity, diffusion, and even temporal progression. We find that injecting these concept directions back into the model during inference enables fine-grained causal control: vortices can be induced or removed, diffusion enhanced or suppressed, and simulations sped up or slowed down. Moreover, directions derived from one physical system also steer the behaviour of other physical systems, suggesting that they are domain-general. These results provide early evidence that scientific foundation models can learn general representations of physical principles, and further support for the Linear Representation Hypothesis.

[228] arXiv:2511.21638 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Iterative Policy Optimization: Batch-Online Multi-Turn RL via Single-Turn RL
Daniel R. Jiang, Ankur Samanta, Yukai Yang, Jalaj Bhandari, Rémi Munos, Tyler Lu
Comments: The first two authors contributed equally
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Practical LLM agents often operate over multi-turn conversations where success is determined only after the full interaction ends. Most multi-turn RL methods train via on-policy rollouts, but unlike in single-turn RL, the policy cannot produce a trajectory alone, since an external environment must respond after each agent turn. For conversational agents, this environment is a user, but real users are generally unavailable inside the training loop and simulated users are difficult to build faithfully. Separately, real-world deployment is rarely fully online or fully offline. The common production pattern is called batch online, where the current policy is deployed to collect a batch of interaction data, then retrained on that batch and redeployed. We show that this batch-online setting creates an opportunity for applying the classical approximate policy iteration algorithm. Our central observation is that running standard token-level, single-turn GRPO with a learned turn-level $Q$-function as the reward model is a policy improvement step for the multi-turn problem. Building on this, we present Iterative Policy Optimization (IterPO), which alternates between fitting $Q^\pi$ from logged Monte Carlo returns via standard reward modeling (policy evaluation) and running single-turn GRPO against $Q^\pi$ (policy improvement). During policy improvement, the learned $Q^\pi$ scores candidate responses by their expected downstream return, avoiding the need for simulator rollouts of the remaining conversation. Overall, this allows us to do principled multi-turn RL using only single-turn RL methods without an interactive environment or user simulator inside the training loop. We demonstrate the effectiveness of IterPO on six multi-turn negotiation environments.

[229] arXiv:2511.22031 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Predicting Public Health Impacts of Electricity Usage
Yejia Liu, Zhifeng Wu, Pengfei Li, Shaolei Ren
Comments: 16 Pages. Accepted to NeurIPS 2025 Workshop on Socially Responsible and Trustworthy Foundation Models (ResponsibleFM)
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

The electric power sector is a leading source of air pollutant emissions, impacting the public health of nearly every community. Although regulatory measures have reduced air pollutants, fossil fuels remain a significant component of the energy supply, highlighting the need for more advanced demand-side approaches to reduce the public health impacts. To enable health-informed demand-side management, we introduce HealthPredictor, a domain-specific AI model that provides an end-to-end pipeline linking electricity use to public health outcomes. The model comprises three components: a fuel mix predictor that estimates the contribution of different generation sources, an air quality converter that models pollutant emissions and atmospheric dispersion, and a health impact assessor that translates resulting pollutant changes into monetized health damages. Across multiple regions in the United States, our health-driven optimization framework yields substantially lower prediction errors in terms of public health impacts than fuel mix-driven baselines. A case study on electric vehicle charging schedules illustrates the public health gains enabled by our method and the actionable guidance it can offer for health-informed energy management. Overall, this work shows how AI models can be explicitly designed to enable health-informed energy management for advancing public health and broader societal well-being. Our datasets and code are released at: this https URL.

[230] arXiv:2512.00791 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Limitations of Using Identical Distributions for Training and Testing When Learning Boolean Functions
Jordi Pérez-Guijarro
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

When the distributions of the training and test data do not coincide, the problem of understanding generalization becomes considerably more complex, prompting a variety of questions. Prior work has shown that, for some fixed learning methods, there are scenarios where training on a distribution different from the test distribution improves generalization. However, these results do not account for the possibility of choosing, for each training distribution, the optimal learning algorithm, leaving open whether the observed benefits stem from the mismatch itself or from suboptimality of the learner. In this work, we address this question. That is, we study whether it is always optimal for the training distribution to be identical to the test distribution when the learner is allowed to be optimally adapted to the training distribution. Surprisingly, when we restrict our attention to efficient learners, i.e., those running in polynomial time, and assume the existence of one-way functions, the answer is negative. In other words, matching the training and test distributions is not always optimal.

[231] arXiv:2512.01421 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Fourier Neural Operators Explained: A Practical Perspective
Valentin Duruisseaux, Jean Kossaifi, Anima Anandkumar
Comments: 104 pages, 29 figures
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Partial differential equations (PDEs) govern a wide variety of dynamical processes in science and engineering, yet obtaining their numerical solutions often requires high-resolution discretizations and repeated evaluations of complex operators, leading to substantial computational costs. Neural operators have recently emerged as a powerful framework for learning mappings between function spaces directly from data, enabling efficient surrogate models for PDE systems. Among these architectures, the Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) has become the most influential and widely adopted due to its elegant spectral formulation, which captures global correlations through learnable transformations in Fourier space while remaining invariant to discretization and resolution. Despite their success, the practical use of FNOs is often hindered by an incomplete understanding among practitioners of their theoretical foundations, practical constraints, and implementation details, which can lead to their incorrect or unreliable application. This work presents a comprehensive and practice-oriented guide to FNOs, unifying their mathematical principles with implementation strategies. We provide an intuitive exposition of the concepts of operator theory and signal processing that underlie the FNO, detail its spectral parameterization and the computational design of all its components, and address common misunderstandings encountered in the literature. The exposition is closely integrated with the NeuralOperator 2.0.0 library, offering modular state-of-the-art implementations that faithfully reflect the theory. By connecting rigorous foundations with practical insight, this guide aims to establish a clear and reliable framework for applying FNOs effectively across diverse scientific and engineering fields.

[232] arXiv:2601.01501 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Advanced Global Wildfire Activity Modeling with Hierarchical Graph ODE
Fan Xu, Wei Gong, Hao Wu, Lilan Peng, Nan Wang, Qingsong Wen, Xian Wu, Kun Wang, Xibin Zhao
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Wildfires, as an integral component of the Earth system, are governed by a complex interplay of atmospheric, oceanic, and terrestrial processes spanning a vast range of spatiotemporal scales. Modeling their global activity on large timescales is therefore a critical yet challenging task. While deep learning has recently achieved significant breakthroughs in global weather forecasting, its potential for global wildfire behavior prediction remains underexplored. In this work, we reframe this problem and introduce the Hierarchical Graph ODE (HiGO), a novel framework designed to learn the multi-scale, continuous-time dynamics of wildfires. Specifically, we represent the Earth system as a multi-level graph hierarchy and propose an adaptive filtering message passing mechanism for both intra- and inter-level information flow, enabling more effective feature extraction and fusion. Furthermore, we incorporate GNN-parameterized Neural ODE modules at multiple levels to explicitly learn the continuous dynamics inherent to each scale. Through extensive experiments on the SeasFire Cube dataset, we demonstrate that HiGO significantly outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on long-range wildfire forecasting. Moreover, its continuous-time predictions exhibit strong observational consistency, highlighting its potential for real-world applications.

[233] arXiv:2601.07442 (replaced) [pdf, other]
Title: Surrogate-based Optimization via Clustering for Box-Constrained Problems
Maaz Ahmad, Iftekhar A. Karimi
Comments: 34 pages, 4 Figures, 8 Tables
Journal-ref: Computers and Chemical Engineering 207 (2026), 109559
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Optimization and Control (math.OC)

Global optimization of large-scale, complex systems such as multi-physics black-box simulations and real-world industrial systems is important but challenging. This work presents a novel Surrogate-Based Optimization framework based on Clustering, SBOC for global optimization of such systems, which can be used with any surrogate modeling technique. At each iteration, it uses a single surrogate model for the entire domain, employs k-means clustering to identify unexplored domain, and exploits a local region around the surrogate optimum to potentially add three new sample points in the domain. SBOC has been tested against sixteen promising benchmarking algorithms using 52 analytical test functions of varying input dimensionalities and shape profiles. It successfully identified a global minimum for most test functions with substantially lower computational effort than other algorithms. It worked especially well on test functions with four or more input variables. It was also among the top six algorithms in approaching a global minimum closely. Overall, SBOC is a robust, reliable, and efficient algorithm for global optimization of box-constrained systems.

[234] arXiv:2601.15158 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Outcome-Based RL Provably Leads Transformers to Reason, but Only With the Right Data
Yuval Ran-Milo, Yotam Alexander, Shahar Mendel, Nadav Cohen
Comments: 94 pages, 7 figures
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI)

Transformers trained via Reinforcement Learning (RL) with outcome-based supervision can spontaneously develop the ability to generate intermediate reasoning steps (Chain-of-Thought). Yet the mechanism by which sparse rewards drive policy gradient to discover such systematic reasoning remains poorly understood. We address this by analyzing the policy gradient dynamics of single-layer linear Transformers on a synthetic graph traversal task that cannot be solved without Chain-of-Thought but admits a simple iterative solution. We prove that despite training solely on final-answer correctness, policy gradient drives the Transformer to converge to a structured, interpretable algorithm that iteratively traverses the graph vertex-by-vertex. We characterize the distributional properties required for this emergence, identifying the critical role of "simple examples": instances requiring fewer reasoning steps. When the training distribution places sufficient mass on these simpler examples, the Transformer learns a generalizable traversal strategy that extrapolates to longer chains; when this mass vanishes, policy gradient learning becomes infeasible. We corroborate our theoretical results through experiments on synthetic data and with real-world language models on mathematical reasoning tasks, validating that our theoretical findings carry over to practical settings.

[235] arXiv:2601.20250 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Fast Statistical Rates for Flow Matching without Curvature Assumptions
Hari Krishna Sahoo, Mudit Gaur, Vaneet Aggarwal
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Information Theory (cs.IT); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

Flow-based generative models have emerged as an efficient alternative to diffusion models. We study the sample complexity of learning a target distribution in Wasserstein distance via flow matching, which learns a velocity field transporting a base distribution to the target. Under exact empirical risk minimization over a fixed network class and standard assumptions on the architecture and data distribution, we show that any squared-loss flow-matching variant including rectified flow with bounded derivatives achieves $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-2})$ sample complexity for the statistical term with the Wasserstein guarantee taking the form $W_2 \le K(\varepsilon + C\varepsilon_{app})$, where $\varepsilon_{app}$ is the approximation error of the network class. This improves upon existing $\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-4})$ guarantees and does not require the Polyak--Lojasiewicz condition in the statistical analysis. Instead, we exploit a structural property of the squared-loss objective - it induces an approximate Bernstein condition that directly ties the variance of the excess loss to the excess risk up to additive approximation-error. This condition enables a localized Rademacher complexity analysis yielding fast $O(1/n)$ rates. The flow-matching schedule enters the leading statistical prefactor through the Lipschitz constant of the pointwise loss, which we characterize explicitly for standard schedules.

[236] arXiv:2601.21471 (replaced) [pdf, other]
Title: Designing Service Systems from Textual Evidence
Ruicheng Ao, Hongyu Chen, Siyang Gao, Hanwei Li, David Simchi-Levi
Comments: Substantially revised and expanded version of arXiv:2601.21471 prepared for journal resubmission, with a new title and the complete Electronic Companion
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Optimization and Control (math.OC); Machine Learning (stat.ML)

In service system design, it is often the case that the main evidence of system performance appears in textual form, such as customer support transcripts, complaint narratives, and compliance review reports. With the increasing use of large language models (LLMs), these textual trajectories can be converted into low-cost proxy scores that support comparison and optimization of candidate service configurations. However, LLM-based evaluations can exhibit systematic bias and require human audits for correction. To this end, this research studies how to identify the best service configuration with high confidence while minimizing the use of expensive human audits. We formulate the problem as fixed-confidence best arm identification with an always-observed, potentially biased proxy and selectively acquired human-verified outcomes. Moreover, several configurations can run on one case. A human audit can provide a case label that scores all their outputs. We show that sharing this reference and deciding whether to audit after observing proxy scores can each strictly reduce asymptotic identification cost. The selected configurations determine the available proxy scores and verified outcomes, so the proposed algorithm allocates configuration evaluations and subsequent audits jointly. For a specified finite family of data-generating models containing the true law and distinguishing different best configurations, its expected cost asymptotically attains the information-theoretic lower bound. For audits of individual outputs, we develop prediction-powered confidence sequences valid under adaptive auditing and delayed feedback. Numerical experiments on synthetic examples and service datasets show that the proposed algorithms require substantially less human review while maintaining reliable selection.

[237] arXiv:2601.22447 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: What Does a Sparse Autoencoder Feature Do? A Weight-Based Account
Yiting Liu, Zhi-Hong Deng
Comments: NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a powerful technique for decomposing language model representations into interpretable features. Current interpretation pipelines infer feature semantics from activation patterns, implicitly assuming every feature has a semantic explanation while overlooking the computational roles features inherit from the SAE training objective. We introduce a weight-based interpretation framework that requires no activation data and grounds claims causally through targeted feature-ablation interventions. Across Gemma-2 and Llama-3.1, three depth-dependent signatures show that SAE features inherit the base model's geometry: semantic features form a U-shape under tied embeddings but bifurcate when untied, attention participation peaks mid-layer, and the two roles couple oppositely for input- vs. output-oriented features. This weight-based view supplies the causal half missing from activation-based interpretability.

[238] arXiv:2602.00513 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Minerva: Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards for Cyber Threat Intelligence LLMs
Md Tanvirul Alam, Aritran Piplai, Ionut Cardei, Nidhi Rastogi, Peter J Worth Jr
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG)

Cyber threat intelligence (CTI) analysts routinely convert noisy, unstructured security artifacts into standardized, automation-ready representations. Although large language models (LLMs) show promise for this task, existing approaches remain brittle when producing structured CTI outputs and have largely relied on supervised fine-tuning (SFT). In contrast, CTI standards and community-maintained resources define canonical identifiers and schemas that enable deterministic verification of model outputs. We leverage this structure to study reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) for CTI tasks. We introduce Minerva, a unified dataset and training pipeline spanning multiple CTI subtasks, each paired with task-specific verifiers that score structured outputs and identifier predictions. To address reward sparsity during rollout, we propose MinervaRL, an auxiliary self-training mechanism that generates additional verified trajectories and distills them back into the model. Averaged across four backbones and 12 CTI benchmarks, MinervaRL improves the mean score by 15.8 percentage points over the corresponding base models and by 4.3 points over GRPO. The project page is available at this https URL.

[239] arXiv:2602.04908 (replaced) [pdf, html, other]
Title: Temporal Pair Consistency for Flow Matching
Chika Maduabuchi, Jindong Wang
Comments: NeurIPS 2026
Subjects: Machine Learning (cs.LG); Artificial Intelligence (cs.AI); Computer Vision and Pattern Recognition (cs.CV)

Flow-matching-style generative models learn time-dependent vector fields, but standard objectives supervise each timestep independently, leaving shared-path temporal structure unused. We introduce Temporal Pair Consistency (TPC), a simple training-time objective that couples velocity predictions at paired timesteps along the same probability path. TPC leaves the architecture, probability path, sampler, and inference-time computation unchanged. Under matched backbones, training budgets, solvers, and numbers of function evaluations, TPC improves sample quality across flow matching, OT-CFM, rectified flow, DiT-style backbones, and MeanFlow. On CIFAR-10, TPC improves FM from 6.35 to 3.19 FID and OT-CFM from 3.58 to 2.90 FID at the same NFE.
